About

I work at the intersection of business, government and academia, shaping thinking on economic growth, productivity and public policy in the UK.

Over three decades, I have advised senior leaders in industry and government on high-stakes strategic questions. I bring together data, analysis and systems thinking to clarify choices and strengthen long-term outcomes, with a particular focus on the implications of artificial intelligence for productivity and labour markets.

Alongside my advisory work, I contribute to national commissions and policy debates and maintain close links with academia. I value intellectual independence, robust evidence, cross-disciplinary thinking and clear communication.

Outside work, I recharge through singing and swimming, and enjoy learning about human psychology, wellbeing and languages.

In an era defined by disruption, the biggest surprise in UK consumer behaviour is how little has changed. Since 2019, households have weathered an extraordinary series of shocks. Yet when examine the data, a striking picture of stability emerges. The one big shift? Home comforts.

Mind the capital gap: British citizens are poorer because UK workers are denied capital - The Productivity Institute

The Productivity Institute

The UK doesn't have a productivity puzzle. A significant proportion of its lower-than-peers productivity level is explained by a simple fact: people employed in the UK have access to 33% less capital per hour worked than those in peer countries. In absolute terms, this means that the UK has a capital gap of £2 trillion. Incremental policies will not unlodge the UK from its low-investment, low-productivity equilibrium. #dataisbeautiful

The UK inflation cycle appears to be nearing its end - what can businesses learn from it? | United Kingdom

McKinsey & Company

UK inflation appears to be stabilising. However, the dynamics remain complex and uncertain. Businesses that learn the lessons of the past and invest in foresight capabilities can build confidence for the future. This article takes a look at the different waves of inflation that added up to the recent record-high price rises and zooms in on the different experiences of specific types of households or businesses. It recommends continued pricing vigilance and agility amidst uncertainty.

What do people think about?

Shanshan Zhang, Zhou Fang, and Josh Tasoff recorded >23,000 thoughts from 258 Americans, who received random phone prompts during a period of 2 weeks asking them to describe what they are thinking about, what they are doing, and how they feel.

So what do people think about most frequently?
1. Senses 19%
2. Work 17%
3. Food 14%
4. Hobbies 10%
5. Relationships 10%
6. Health 8%
7. Chores 7%
8. Self 6%
9. Financial 3%
10. World 3% (particularly Ukraine, see Fig C6 in the Appendix)

The Figures below show some more fascinating details.

The panel with gray bars shows who we think about when we think about relations.
From top to bottom:
1. Friend
2. Dog
3. Son
4. Mother
5. Cat
6. Daughter
7. Boyfriend
8. Wife
9. Husband
10. Coworker
11. Girlfriend
12. Father
13. Sister
14. Brother

The colorful panels with word clouds show what we most frequently want, need, feel, worry, love, and hate.

Why study thoughts? One reason is that thoughts are strongly predictive of people's self-reported happiness: "Thoughts explain more of happiness than what people are doing, demographics, and socio-economic status combined".

Important caveat: reporting is selective! The authors note: "we were surprised by how rarely sex appeared in people’s thoughts. In our entire data set, sex appeared only 11 times" "Future studies should measure sexual and romantic thoughts more directly while preserving privacy."

A lot more results and analyses in the paper.

Read the full paper here:

Shanshan Zhang, Zhou Fang, and Joshua Tasof (2026), What do people think about?, working paper:
https://lnkd.in/eYGFgCTN

1w • 

Your parents' happiness at age X is quite predictive of your happiness at age X.

The figure below shows the gap between child's life satisfaction and parents' life satisfaction measured at the same age. Almost 25% of children experience the same life satisfaction as their parents did at the same age. Another 35% is very close to it, with slightly more people to the right (more happy) than to the left (less happy).

The figure is from a new paper by Andrew Clark and Anthony LEPINTEUR studying intergenerational transmission of well-being using rich panel data from the UK:
https://lnkd.in/d53Y-6JE

The intergenerational transmission of well-being appears to be slightly weaker than the intergenerational transmission of income. Also, part of it remains after controlling for income, suggesting that "well-being persistence is different from economic persistence".

Interestingly, the paper also finds that "well-being is transmitted across generations not only in levels, but also in terms of the way in which it changes over the life cycle".

This is the Abstract:

"There are many estimates of the intergenerational transmission of income and education, even though these may be considered as only partial measures of individual welfare. We here analyse  long-running UK panel data and directly consider the intergenerational transmission of two widely-used indicators of well-being, life satisfaction and psychological distress. We use the long run nature of this panel data to construct parent–child dyads who are observed at the same age, and so avoid the life-cycle bias that appears in much existing work on intergenerational correlation.  We find that well-being is transmitted across generations, but to a lesser extent than are income and education. Observed economic outcomes only slightly mediate this relationship, and the estimated transmission is similar across different types of parents and children. Exploiting the panel structure of the data, where both parents and their children are observed repeatedly over time, we show that well-being is transmitted across generations not only in levels, but also in terms of the way in which it changes over the life cycle."

Read the full paper here:
Andrew Clark and Anthony LEPINTEUR (2026), The Intergenerational Correlation of Subjective Well-Being, Paris School of Economics working paper:
https://lnkd.in/d53Y-6JE

Fear of failure may be holding back more than football - it could also be shaping the UK’s investment challenge.

Tera Allas CBE and Stephen Roper were featured in The Times last week, drawing on their research into UK managers’ attitudes to ambition, risk and investment.

Their findings show that UK managers are no less ambitious than their international peers, but are more risk-averse and more sensitive to potential losses. This adds important evidence to the debate on why business investment remains low in the UK.

As the article highlights, understanding these attitudes is vital if we are to unlock greater investment, innovation and productivity growth.

What if the UK’s investment challenge is less about ambition, and more about risk?

A recent report by Tera Allas CBE and Stephen Roper explores whether the attitudes of those making investment decisions may be contributing to the UK’s persistent business investment gap.

Drawing on 34 survey items from five cross-national datasets, the report compares UK managers with managers in 15 peer economies across six attitudes and behaviours linked to investment decisions.

The analysis suggests that UK managers are not less ambitious than their international counterparts. However, they are:
• More prone to satisficing - accepting “good enough” outcomes
• Consistently more risk and loss averse
• Showing some evidence of greater ambiguity aversion and short-termism

The result is a distinct UK manager profile: ambitious but risk averse.

The findings suggest that closing the UK’s investment gap may require more than financial incentives. Businesses also need the confidence to invest, supported by a more stable policy environment, reduced exposure to potential losses, and support for managers to make informed decisions about risk.

Read the full report on our website: https://lnkd.in/e3X-urq3
Listen to Tera Allas CBE and Stephen Roper discuss this on our latest podcast: https://lnkd.in/e3kGRBU3
